title: Rethinking Projector Training in Multimodal LLMs

paper.title: Rethinking Projector Training in Multimodal LLMs
paper.abstract:
Abstract Multimodal LLMs are typically trained by first aligning a vision encoder with a language model via projector training on large image-caption datasets, followed by joint training of the full multimodal model.
Despite its widespread use, the role of the projector training stage remains poorly understood.
We find that (i) using only 10 10 to 20 % 20\% of the data for training the projector already recovers most downstream performance gains, and (ii) projectors trained on different datasets can be linearly interpolated while largely preserving performance.
These results suggest that projector training mainly performs a coarse alignment, which many different projectors achieve equally well.
Motivated by these findings, we propose PORTAL , a training-free projector initialization that requires neither paired image-caption data nor gradient-based optimization , but only per-modality summary statistics. PORTAL computes an optimal-transport-based map between Gaussian approximations of the vision and language feature distributions on a shared principal subspace, so that the projector training stage can be skipped entirely.
Without any paired data, PORTAL matches the standard pipeline trained on 558k image-caption pairs across six LLM backbones, two vision encoders, and 16 benchmarks. It outperforms that pipeline in 3 3 of 7 7 (vision encoder, LLM) settings and reaches an average 98 % 98\% of its score across the other four.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Modern multimodal LLMs commonly align a vision encoder with a language model by first training a projector on a large amount of image-caption paired samples, followed by joint training of the full multimodal model. This pipeline has become standard, from LLaVA [ 1 , 2 ] , Molmo [ 3 ] , and InternVL [ 4 ] to the QwenVL series [ 5 ] . While the first stage of projector alignment has been motivated by the goal of producing a visual tokenizer compatible with the frozen LLM [ 1 ] , what this stage actually does remains poorly understood. Prior works offer conflicting evidence: Prismatic [ 6 ] reports that skipping projector alignment can improve performance, whereas Cambrian-1 [ 7 ] shows that scaling the training data of projector alignment to 2.5M image-caption pairs helps. MM1 [ 8 ] suggests that factors like resolution and data mixing matter more than the projector design. These findings are difficult to reconcile without a deeper understanding of what projector alignment actually does. In this work, we show that projector alignment primarily performs coarse alignment , mapping visual features into a language-model-compatible input space which admits a large set of possible solutions. Two empirical observations support this view: (i) using only 10 10 to 20 % 20\% of the standard 558 558 k-sample alignment corpus achieves similar performance to training on the full dataset, and (ii) projectors trained on entirely different datasets can be linearly interpolated without losing performance. If the projector alignment learned a precise and semantically unique mapping, neither reducing the training data nor linear interpolation between independently trained projectors would preserve performance. Figure 1 : Projector alignment as a coarse alignment with a broad solution space. ( Left ) Standard pipeline: during projector alignment, the vision encoder and language model are frozen, and only the projector is trained to map visual tokens into a representation space compatible with the LLM using image-caption pairs. ( Middle ) We show that projectors trained on different image-caption datasets can be linearly interpolated while largely preserving downstream performance, indicating that there is a large solution space for the weights of the projector. ( Right ) This observation motivates a closed-form solution of projector alignment. We propose a training-free projector PORTAL constructed by optimal transport between the two modalities’ marginal statistics. Motivated by these observations, we propose PORTAL ( P rojector via O ptimal-transpo RT AL ignment), a training-free approach that constructs the projector from the marginal statistics of the two modalities. PORTAL is the Bures-Wasserstein optimal transport map between Gaussian approximations of the vision feature distribution and the language-model input distribution, computed in a shared top- k k principal subspace. It does not require any paired captions or gradient-based optimization , relying only on the per-modality means, principal directions, and the spread along each direction. PORTAL removes the projector alignment training stage entirely. Across seven (vision encoder, LLM) pairs spanning four LLM families (Vicuna, LLaMA, Qwen, OLMo) from 0.5B to 8B parameters, and two vision encoders (CLIP, SigLIP), PORTAL matches the standard pipeline trained on 558 558 k image-caption pairs and exceeds it in three out of seven settings, peaking at 106 % 106\% of the trained baseline. When PORTAL is used to initialize rather than replace projector alignment, the performance of the baseline is reached with 135 × 135\times fewer alignment FLOPs. Performance gaps are concentrated on OCR-heavy benchmarks, where marginal statistics appear insufficient to capture fine-grained character-level spatial structure that paired supervision provides.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Projector alignment in multimodal LLMs. Two-stage multimodal LLM training, where a vision encoder is first aligned to a frozen language model via training a projector, followed by visual instruction tuning, has become a standard pipeline for training multimodal LLMs. This pipeline was popularized by LLaVA [ 1 , 2 ] and replicated in InstructBLIP [ 9 ] , BLIP-2 [ 10 ] , Flamingo [ 11 ] , Molmo [ 3 ] , InternVL [ 4 ] , and the Qwen-VL series [ 5 ] . Despite its success, the role of Stage-I projector alignment has been poorly understood and prior studies offer conflicting views. Prismatic finds it can be skipped without a loss [ 6 ] . Cambrian-1 reports that scaling Stage-I data to 2.5M pairs helps [ 7 ] . MM1 emphasizes resolution and data mixing over the projector itself [ 8 ] . We resolve this disagreement by identifying what projector alignment actually does: Stage-I acts as geometric conditioning of visual features into the LLM input distribution , not as fine-grained semantic learning. This explains the three findings above as a single phenomenon: skipping Stage-I works when the projector already lands in a compatible region (Prismatic [ 6 ] ), more data helps only until that region is reached (Cambrian-1 [ 7 ] ), and the resolution and data mixing dominate because they affect the conditioning more than the projector capacity does (MM1 [ 8 ] ). These findings lead us to propose a closed-form projector that requires neither paired data nor gradient updates. Connector designs and projector geometry. Beyond the MLP used in LLaVA [ 1 ] , connector architectures span the Q-Former [ 10 ] , Perceiver Resampler [ 11 ] , locality-enhanced abstractors [ 12 ] , ALIGN [ 13 ] , vision-expert mixtures [ 14 ] , prefix-attention adapters [ 15 ] , and pixel-shuffle or patch-merging schemes for token reduction [ 16 , 5 ] . A complementary line of work analyzes what these connectors actually do. Verma et al. [17] track how visual information degrades through LLM layers, Li et al. [18] probe information loss through learned projectors, Li and others [19] report systematic norm discrepancies between visual and text tokens, and Shukor and Cord [20] show that cross-modal alignment emerges primarily after self-attention layers. We use the 2-layer MLP projector of LLaVA by default, and also test PORTAL with a linear projector and with the C-Abstractor [ 12 ] , which has 19 × 19\times more parameters (Section 5.3 ). Optimal transport for feature alignment. The Bures-Wasserstein optimal transport map between two Gaussians has a closed form on positive-definite covariances [ 21 , 22 ] , which the construction of the projector in our work exploits. Courty et al. [23] introduced OT for domain adaptation, and Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola [24] used Gromov-Wasserstein to align word-embedding spaces with no paired anchors. Closest to PORTAL is CORAL [ 25 , 26 ] , which aligns second-order statistics with a single linear map for domain adaptation. PORTAL extends this idea to the multimodal-alignment setting and ties it explicitly to the Bures-Wasserstein optimum on a shared top- k k principal subspace, which we then use as a closed-form projector rather than a regularizer. Training-free and efficient connector construction. Several recent works try to eliminate or reduce connector training. VPGTrans [ 27 ] transfers a learned visual prompt generator across LLMs at reduced cost. LangBridge [ 28 ] interprets visual tokens as combinations of language embeddings, enabling cross-LLM transfer at the price of bottlenecking visual information through a vocabulary subspace. SEMI [ 29 ] meta-learns a hypernetwork connector that adapts to new modalities from a few samples. In the related CLIP-classification setting, training-free or lightweight adapters such as Tip-Adapter [ 30 ] and TaskRes [ 31 ] cache or residualize over a frozen backbone. PORTAL differs from all of the above by requiring neither paired data, gradient steps, learned caches, nor a vocabulary bottleneck: it is a closed-form construction from per-modality summary statistics alone. Gupta et al. [32] also learn without paired multimodal data, but to improve a unimodal representation by sharing parameters across unpaired modalities, whereas we ask whether the projector between a frozen vision encoder and a frozen LLM needs paired training at all.

sections.heading: 3.1 Projector Alignment Saturates with a Small Number of Samples
sections.text: To investigate the role of projector alignment, we first examine how downstream performance scales with the amount of Stage-I training data. If strong performance requires large-scale data, it would suggest the projector is learning fine-grained visual-language correspondences. Conversely, if a small fraction of the data is sufficient, this would indicate that the projector primarily learns a coarse-grained correspondence, placing visual features into a broadly compatible input space for the language model. We conduct this analysis on the LLaVA 1.5 setup (CLIP ViT-L/14-336, Vicuna 1.5 7B, 2-layer MLP projector), with LCS-558k for Stage-I and LLaVA-665k for Stage-II. For the data-fraction experiment we replace Vicuna with MobileLLaMA 1.4B, which keeps 11 data fractions on two corpora tractable. We evaluate on 16 benchmarks grouped into four categories adapted from the Cambrian-1 [ 7 ] taxonomy: Knowledge (Know.), General (Gen.), OCR, and Vision-Centric (Vis.). Appendix C lists the benchmarks in each. Full experimental details are in Appendix C.1 . (a) LCS-558k (b) ShareGPT-1.2M Figure 2 : Stage-I gain saturates early. Relative gain in downstream performance over the no-pretraining baseline by Cambrian-1 category, as a function of Stage-I data fraction on LCS-558k (left) and ShareGPT-1.2M (right). OCR and Chart benefit the most, while Knowledge and Vision-Centric scores saturate early. We observe that only 10 10 to 20 % 20\% of the LCS-558k image-caption pairs already capture most of the downstream benefit, and all categories plateau by 30 30 to 40 % 40\% (Figure 2 ). The marginal downstream benefit of the remaining pairs is small under this protocol. ShareGPT-1.2M, more than twice as large, does not do better: its average peaks at 38.1 38.1 with 40 % 40\% of its data (Appendix D ). These results suggest that projector alignment is not primarily learning fine-grained visual-language correspondences. Rather, it appears to perform a coarse-grained alignment step, mapping visual features into a region of the LLM input space from which subsequent joint training can effectively adapt the full multimodal model.

sections.heading: 3.2 Projector Alignment Admits a Broad Solution Space
sections.text: We have shown that projector alignment can be achieved with only a small fraction of the standard pretraining data. This observation is consistent with two possible explanations: either the set of effective projector solutions is narrow but easy to reach, or the solution space itself is broad. To distinguish between these possibilities, we examine whether independently trained projectors can be linearly interpolated while preserving performance. If effective projectors occupied a narrow and isolated region, interpolation would be expected to degrade performance. Instead, we find that projectors along the entire interpolation path largely preserve downstream performance, supporting the view that projector alignment admits a broad solution space (Figure 3 ). The per-category breakdown results further support this interpretation. The cross-data interpolation path is not only traversable but often outperforms either endpoint. Averaged across the four Cambrian-1 categories, every interior α \alpha improves on both LCS-558k and ShareGPT-1.2M projectors, with the optimum at α = 0.5 \alpha{=}0.5 . The category-wise optima differ: OCR peaks closer to the ShareGPT endpoint, Knowledge closer to the LCS endpoint. The aggregate score improves with mixing, so a simple combination of two independently trained solutions, with no additional Stage-I optimization, outperforms both. Such behavior indicates that projector alignment admits a broad solution space. The two projectors above start from the same initialization and differ only in their training data. We next asked whether the initialization matters in the same way, and trained a second pair on the same LCS-558k data from two different random initializations. Unlike the cross-data pair, this cross-seed pair is not linearly interpolable: captioning CIDEr drops from about 80 80 at both endpoints to 0.7 0.7 at α = 0.5 \alpha{=}0.5 (Appendix C.2 ). Initialization thus appears to select the loss basin, and training data the solution within it. These results clarify the role of projector alignment. The early saturation with limited data and the traversable interpolation path between projectors trained on different data suggest that projector alignment does not require a highly specific solution. Instead, projector alignment appears to place visual features into a broadly compatible region of the LLM input space, where many different projector weights can serve the same functional role.

sections.heading: 4 PORTAL: Training-Free Projector via Optimal Transport
sections.text: The previous findings suggest that projector alignment primarily serves as geometric conditioning, placing visual features into a region of the LLM input space from which subsequent joint training can effectively adapt the multimodal model. This mapping admits a large set of solutions, motivating a simpler alternative to the projector alignment training stage. We instantiate this idea with PORTAL ( P rojector via O ptimal-transpo RT AL ignment), a training-free method that initializes the projector from the marginal feature statistics of the vision encoder and the LLM. PORTAL estimates the mean, principal directions, and variances of each modality separately, then constructs a closed-form optimal-transport map that aligns the source visual feature distribution with a compatible target language-feature distribution. We also show why matching only means and covariances can suffice. The LLM normalizes each token before attention, so attention depends only on token directions. When token norms vary little, the spread of these directions is fixed by the covariance, which PORTAL matches.

sections.heading: 5.1 PORTAL Matches Trained Projector Alignment Without Paired Data
sections.text: We find that our closed-form projector PORTAL requiring no paired captions or gradient updates achieves comparable downstream performance to conventional alignment pipelines trained on 558k image-caption pairs, across a range of vision encoder and LLM combinations (Table 1 ). In particular, using LLaMA 3.2 1B/CLIP and Qwen 2.5 0.5B/CLIP, PORTAL reaches 106.2 % \mathbf{106.2\%} and 106.1 % \mathbf{106.1\%} of the trained baseline, respectively. Using LLaMA 3.1 8B/CLIP, it exceeds the trained baseline, reaching 102.7 % \mathbf{102.7\%} . On Vicuna 1.5 with CLIP and SigLIP, Qwen 2.5 7B, and OLMo 2 1B, PORTAL remains very close to the trained projector, reaching 98.8 % 98.8\% , 99.3 % 99.3\% , 98.3 % 98.3\% , and 96.3 % 96.3\% of the trained baseline, respectively. Thus, PORTAL removes the requirement for paired training data and optimization cost of projector alignment while preserving almost all of its downstream benefit after instruction tuning. The advantage of PORTAL is clearest where the random projector fails. On SigLIP, the Random baseline collapses to 82.5 % \mathbf{82.5\%} of the trained projector. PORTAL closes that gap to 99.3 % \mathbf{99.3\%} . This is what we would expect if the alignment stage were dominated by distributional matching rather than caption supervision. Two settings sit below the trained baseline’s bootstrap CI, Qwen 2.5 7B/CLIP and OLMo 2 1B/CLIP, with the gaps concentrated on OCR and Chart benchmarks. This matches the observation in Section 3.1 that OCR and Chart drive most of the Stage-I gain over the no-pretraining baseline, supporting our reading that character-level spatial structure is the regime where paired captions teach what marginal statistics alone cannot recover. Importantly, this phenomenon is not specific to PORTAL. Other unpaired distribution-matching approaches, including CORAL [ 26 ] and Gromov-Wasserstein [ 24 ] alignment, also recover most of the performance of paired Stage-I training (Appendix E.1 ). This provides additional evidence that much of the benefit of Stage-I can be obtained by bringing the two modalities into a compatible feature distribution, rather than requiring a uniquely learned image-text correspondence. A category-level analysis across all seven configurations further shows that this behavior is not systematic across OCR tasks: PORTAL retains, on average, 100.7%, 102.0%, 102.4%, and 100.4% of the trained-baseline performance on Knowledge, General, OCR, and Vision-Centric tasks, respectively (Appendix E.2 ). We further test PORTAL beyond the standard LLaVA-665k Stage-II setting. Under substantially larger-scale multimodal instruction tuning with 3.2M samples, PORTAL slightly outperforms the conventionally Stage-I-trained initialization (Appendix E.3 ). We also evaluate object hallucination on POPE [ 43 ] and find that PORTAL matches or exceeds the trained Stage-I baseline in every setting (Appendix E.4 ).

sections.heading: 5.2 PORTAL Reduces the Projector Alignment Budget
sections.text: Figure 4 : Alignment compute efficiency on Vicuna 1.5 7B/CLIP. Average over the 16 benchmarks as a function of the projector alignment budget, with identical Stage-II tuning on LLaVA-665k. PORTAL stays above Random at every budget. The marked point indicates the crossover at roughly 4 4 k captions, where PORTAL matches the 558 558 k-trained baseline at ∼ \sim 135 × 135{\times} fewer alignment FLOPs. The horizontal dashed line shows the 558 558 k baseline. The previous experiment shows that PORTAL can provide a strong projector without paired optimization. We next ask whether PORTAL can also serve as a warm start for projector alignment. Instead of using PORTAL to skip this stage entirely, we initialize the projector with PORTAL and then continue projector alignment with progressively smaller subsets of LCS-558k. This experiment evaluates whether closed-form alignment can reduce the amount of paired data needed for subsequent projector training. We vary the projector alignment budget over { 0 , 1 ​ k , 10 ​ k , 100 ​ k , 558 ​ k } \{0,1\text{k},10\text{k},100\text{k},558\text{k}\} paired captions from LCS-558k on Vicuna 1.5 7B/CLIP, starting from either a Random or a PORTAL projector. The 0 0 point skips projector alignment entirely and proceeds directly to Stage-II from the initialization, and the 558 558 k point is the standard LLaVA baseline. Stage-II tuning on LLaVA-665k is identical for every configuration. PORTAL provides a better starting point at every projector alignment budget than the random initialization (Figure 4 ). With zero projector training, it already outperforms random initialization. As more paired captions are added, the PORTAL-initialized projector remains consistently above the randomly initialized projector. PORTAL reaches the performance of the full 558k trained projector baseline using only around 4k captions, corresponding to roughly 𝟏𝟑𝟓 × \mathbf{135{\times}} fewer projector alignment FLOPs. Beyond matching the trained baseline at lower compute, PORTAL with as few as 10k paired captions exceeds the full 558k-trained projector baseline and continues to widen the gap up to 100k. PORTAL therefore offers two practical advantages: it reaches the trained baseline at substantially lower alignment cost, and it surpasses that baseline once even a small paired-data budget is available. This result strengthens the main claim that much of projector alignment is a distributional conditioning problem. The projector has a large solution space, and many mappings can make visual features compatible with the LLM input space. PORTAL identifies one such compatible solution directly in closed form. This solution is not necessarily the exact optimum selected by supervised projector training but it lies close to the high-performing region, providing strong performance without paired optimization and a small amount of paired data can further refine it within this region. Additional projector training thus mainly refines a projector that is already compatible.

We therefore test whether its gains persist when the projector is simplified and when the unlabeled image pool used to estimate vision-side statistics is changed. For architecture, we replace the standard 2-layer MLP-GELU projector with a single linear layer, keeping all other components fixed (Table 2 ). If PORTAL’s gains depended on the expressivity of the MLP, they should weaken in this setting. Instead, the gain becomes larger. With the MLP projector, PORTAL reaches 106.2 % \mathbf{106.2\%} of the trained baseline against Random’s 99.9 % 99.9\% . With the linear projector, it reaches 111.8 % \mathbf{111.8\%} against Random’s 94.2 % 94.2\% , widening the Random-to-PORTAL gap from 6.3 6.3 to 17.6 17.6 percentage points. This shows that PORTAL’s advantage does not come from a particular nonlinearity or hidden expansion. It comes from placing the visual features into a better-matched LLM input distribution. We also test the opposite regime by substantially increasing connector capacity. Using the C-Abstractor [ 12 ] , which contains approximately 19 × 19\times more parameters than the two-layer MLP and additionally performs token mixing and sequence compression, PORTAL remains essentially indistinguishable from conventional Stage-I training (42.93 vs. 42.98 average score; Appendix E.5 ). The small drop at k = 1024 k{=}1024 is consistent with noisy eigenvectors diluting the transport map. We adopt k = 512 k{=}512 as the default.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: This work rethinks projector alignment in multimodal LLMs. Our results suggest that this stage primarily performs coarse alignment, mapping visual features into a language-model-compatible input space rather than learning fine-grained visual-language correspondences. This view is supported by the early saturation of alignment data, where 10 to 20% of LCS-558k recovers most downstream gains, and by the linear interpolability of projectors trained on different datasets from a shared initialization. Motivated by this finding, we introduced PORTAL, a training-free projector initialization. PORTAL uses only per-modality summary statistics, requires no paired image-caption data or gradient-based optimization, and remains close to the 558k-trained baseline across the evaluated model pairs. As an initialization, it reaches the trained baseline with roughly 135 × 135\times lower alignment compute. These results suggest that projector alignment can often be replaced by, or reduced to, a lightweight feature-distribution matching step, lowering the cost and paired-data requirements for building multimodal LLMs. Several natural directions remain for future work. Our study focuses on projector alignment with frozen vision and language backbones during alignment, single-image inputs, and simple projector architectures. Extending the analysis to richer connectors, long-context grounding, multi-image reasoning, and additional modalities such as audio, video, and 3D would further clarify how broadly this coarse-alignment view applies. We discuss other limitations of PORTAL in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Appendix A Limitations
sections.text: Our analysis and method address a specific slice of the multimodal-LLM pipeline: Stage-I projector alignment with frozen vision and language backbones. Several caveats follow from that scope. (i) The empirical analysis in Section 3 runs on the LLaVA 1.5 architecture with a 2-layer MLP projector. Richer connectors (resamplers, perceiver-style cross-attention, multi-stage abstractors) may not exhibit the same linear interpolability, and we do not test them here. (ii) PORTAL is constructed from a Gaussian approximation of each modality. The approximation captures means, principal directions, and per-axis spread, but no higher-order structure. Appendix H.1 quantifies how far real source and target distributions deviate from this assumption. We hypothesize that the residual gap on OCR and Chart benchmarks reflects this missing higher-order structure (character-level spatial layout). (iii) As in LLaVA-1.5, all experiments keep the vision encoder frozen and train only the projector and the LLM in Stage-II. We do not study end-to-end fine-tuning that also updates the vision encoder. (iv) Our 16-benchmark suite follows the Cambrian-1 grouping and inherits its biases. It does not stress long-context grounding or multi-image reasoning, which may behave differently. (v) We instantiate PORTAL for vision-to-language alignment. We have not tested it on audio or video encoders. The present results should be regarded as a first existence proof rather than a finished construction. (vi) Our reading of Stage-I as geometric conditioning is the simplest hypothesis consistent with our data. We do not claim it is the unique mechanism, and other interpretations remain possible. (vii) The closed-form construction exceeds trained Stage-I or stays within 1.6 1.6 average points of it across the configurations we test. We make no broader claim that this holds across all multimodal-LLM regimes. Richer benchmarks or backbones may reveal regimes where trained Stage-I genuinely outperforms PORTAL.

The data-fraction experiment in Section 3.1 uses the smaller MobileLLaMA 1.4B backbone [ 61 ] with a 1024 → 2048 → 2048 1024\to 2048\to 2048 projector to keep the 11 11 data fractions on two corpora computationally feasible. For two corpora, LCS-558k and ShareGPT-1.2M, we train Stage-I projectors at evenly spaced data fractions ( 0 0 to 100 % 100\% ), apply identical LLaVA-665k instruction tuning on each, and evaluate on 16 16 benchmarks grouped into the four Cambrian-1 categories (Knowledge, General, OCR, Vision-Centric).

sections.heading: C.2 Cross-Seed vs. Cross-Data Interpolation
sections.text: Section 3.2 reports that projectors trained on different datasets from the same initialization remain interpolable along the linear interpolation path. This appendix complements that result with a control that varies the random initialization instead of the training data, and contrasts the two cases.

sections.text: We train two pairs of projectors using the LLaVA 1.5 setup described in Appendix C.1 . Cross-data projectors share the same random initialization but are trained on different corpora (LCS-558k and ShareGPT-1.2M). Cross-seed projectors share the LCS-558k corpus but use two different random initializations. For each pair ( W A , W B ) (W_{A},W_{B}) we report the Frobenius distance ‖ W A − W B ‖ F \|W_{A}-W_{B}\|_{F} and evaluate the linear interpolation W α = ( 1 − α ) ​ W A + α ​ W B W_{\alpha}=(1-\alpha)\,W_{A}+\alpha\,W_{B} for α ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \alpha\in[0,1] . sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: The cross-seed pair is farther apart in weight space than the cross-data pair ( ‖ Δ ​ W ‖ F = 92.4 \|\Delta W\|_{F}=92.4 versus 63.7 63.7 ), but only the cross-data pair stays inside a low-loss region under interpolation. Cross-seed CIDEr [ 62 ] on the LLaVA captioning evaluation collapses from approximately 80 80 at the two endpoints to 0.7 0.7 at α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 . Cross-data projectors interpolate smoothly along the entire path and the aggregate downstream score peaks at α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 (Figure 3 ).

sections.heading: Interpretation.
sections.text: Cross-seed projectors reach distinct loss basins separated by high-loss barriers, which is the standard picture for independently initialized networks [ 63 ] . Cross-data projectors trained from the same initialization remain inside one shared low-loss region. Initialization therefore selects the basin, and training data selects the particular solution reached within that basin. This is the property that PORTAL targets directly: the closed-form construction lands inside the same compatible region without using paired data.

sections.heading: E.5 Higher-Capacity Connector
sections.text: Our main experiments use either a two-layer MLP or a linear projector. A possible alternative explanation for the observed coarse-alignment behavior is therefore that it arises from limited projector capacity. To test this, we additionally evaluate PORTAL with the C-Abstractor connector from Honeybee [ 12 ] , a substantially higher-capacity architecture that performs both token mixing and sequence compression. In the LLaMA-3.2-1B + CLIP setting, C-Abstractor contains 120.2M parameters, approximately 19 × 19\times more than the 6.3M-parameter two-layer MLP, and compresses the visual sequence from 576 to 144 tokens. We initialize the residual branches of C-Abstractor to zero such that the connector initially reduces to applying PORTAL to the pooled visual features. All remaining C-Abstractor parameters are then optimized during the same Stage-II training used for the other initialization schemes. As shown in Table 14 , PORTAL reaches an average score of 42.93, compared with 42.98 for conventional Stage-I training, while direct Stage-II training from random initialization reaches only 41.46. PORTAL also outperforms the Stage-I-trained baseline on 7 of the 16 individual benchmarks. Thus, increasing connector capacity by approximately 19 × 19\times , while additionally enabling token mixing and sequence compression, does not yield an aggregate advantage for paired Stage-I training over PORTAL. Together with our linear and two-layer MLP experiments, this result provides evidence that the observed coarse-alignment behavior cannot be explained simply by insufficient projector capacity. sections.heading: Interpretation.
sections.text: Read right to left, V_s.T projects each centered source token onto the source’s top- k k principal axes, the diagonal rescaling diag(sigma_t / sigma_s) rescales each axis from source to target spread, and V_t rotates the result into the target’s top- k k principal frame. Adding b1 = mu_t - W1 @ mu_s then recenters to the target mean. The composition matches first and second moments of source and target on the k k -dimensional shared subspace. We use k = 512 k{=}512 as the default (Appendix K ). The construction is well-defined for any k ≤ min ⁡ ( d s , d t , N s , N t ) k\leq\min(d_{s},d_{t},N_{s},N_{t}) .

sections.heading: Cost.
sections.text: The procedure runs two thin SVDs and two matrix multiplies. For the default setting ( N s ≈ 1024 ⋅ 576 N_{s}\!\approx\!1024\cdot 576 , d s = 1024 d_{s}=1024 , d t = 4096 d_{t}=4096 , k = 512 k=512 ) the construction completes in under 30 30 seconds on a single RTX 3090 (Appendix B ) and uses no captions, no paired data, and no gradient steps. This stands in contrast to standard Stage-I projector training, which consumes a paired image-caption corpus (typically LCS-558k) and about 2,200 2{,}200 optimizer steps ( 558 558 k pairs at batch size 256 256 ).

sections.heading: Appendix G Contextualized Targets: Methodology Details
sections.text: This appendix provides the implementation details behind PORTAL-ctx ℓ \ell (Section 4 ).

sections.heading: Probe corpus.
sections.text: We use the concepts.txt corpus released with LatentLens [ 64 ] , a list of English concepts originally assembled for probing latent directions in LLMs. The corpus offers broad semantic coverage and is not tied to any downstream task, which makes it a representative sample of the input distribution of the LLM at depth ℓ \ell .

sections.heading: Cached hidden states.
sections.text: For LLMs covered by LatentLens (LLaMA 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Gemma 2 9B) we use the pre-computed hidden states distributed on Hugging Face. For each LLM and each layer ℓ \ell , the cache stores the post-block- ℓ \ell hidden state of every token in every concepts.txt entry, collected in a single tensor 𝐇 ( ℓ ) ∈ ℝ N t × d t \mathbf{H}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{t}\times d_{t}} . The available layers are ℓ ∈ { 1 , 4 , 8 , 12 , 16 , 20 } \ell\in\{1,4,8,12,16,20\} . For Vicuna v1.5, which is not part of the LatentLens release, we run concepts.txt through the model and store the corresponding hidden states in the same format. The tensor 𝐇 ( ℓ ) \mathbf{H}^{(\ell)} replaces the LLM’s input embedding table as the target distribution in Eq. ( 2 ). The remainder of the PORTAL construction is unchanged.

sections.heading: Layer indexing.
sections.text: ℓ \ell denotes the residual stream after the ℓ \ell -th transformer block (1-indexed), following the LatentLens convention. The setting ℓ = 0 \ell{=}0 recovers standard PORTAL targeting the LLM’s input embedding table.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: No measured distribution is exactly Gaussian, and the Anderson-Darling test rejects Gaussianity on almost all top marginals. This is expected for high-dimensional learned features and does not, on its own, imply that PORTAL should fail. The question is where the deviation lives. Skewness is small for every distribution ( b 1 / k 3 ≤ 0.003 b_{1}/k^{3}\leq 0.003 ), so the residual deviation from Gaussianity lies in tail weight. The tails are heaviest for the vision features (excess kurtosis 0.28 0.28 to 0.49 0.49 ) and light for the LLM input embedding tables ( 0.07 0.07 to 0.13 0.13 ). A second question is whether the distributions that PORTAL targets spread their variance over many directions. The input embedding tables do, with d eff d_{\mathrm{eff}} between 830 830 and 1,713 1{,}713 , while the CLIP patches concentrate their variance in a few directions ( d eff = 4.5 d_{\mathrm{eff}}=4.5 ).

sections.heading: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.text: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes, all claims are placed against related work (Section 2 ) and all claims regarding the method’s performance are backed by empirical results (Section 5 ). Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes, the paper discusses limitations in the Conclusion and in Appendix A . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. • The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. • The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes, Proposition 1 states its assumptions, and Appendix H.2 gives the complete proof. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes, experimental details are described in the experimental setup (Section 5 ), and all hyperparameters and the evaluation protocol are given in Appendices B and C . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. • Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes, the code is available at https://github.com/mlbio-epfl/PORTAL . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. • Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark). • The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. • The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. • At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). • Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes, experimental details are described in the experimental setup (Section 5 ), and all hyperparameters and the evaluation protocol are given in Appendices B and C . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. • The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes, all aggregate scores in the main results and ablation tables are reported with 95 % 95\% confidence intervals computed from B = 1,000 B{=}1{,}000 paired bootstrap resamples [ 60 ] ; resampling is paired across methods within each (encoder, LLM) group so the intervals reflect method differences rather than sample noise. The ± \pm subscripts in the tables denote the half-width of these CIs. The bootstrap protocol is described in Appendix C . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. • The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. • For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). • If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes, we specify the computational resources in Appendix B . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. • The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. • The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines ? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes, we have carefully reviewed and adhered to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. • If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics. • The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes, the positive societal impact of the paper is discussed in the introduction and conclusion. Negative societal impacts are not expected as the outlined methodology enables multimodal LLMs projector alignment without paired data while being computationally efficient. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. • If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. • Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. • The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. • The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. • If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: This paper poses no such risks as beyond code, we are not releasing any new artifacts such as data or models. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. • Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. • Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. • We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes, we cite the creators of every model and dataset we use (Section 5 , Appendices B and C ), and Table 5 lists the license of each dataset. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. • The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. • The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL. • The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. • For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. • If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset. • For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. • If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators. 13. New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [N/A] Justification: This paper does not release any new assets beyond code, which is adequately documented in order to reproduce all results from the paper. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. • Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc. • The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used. • At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file. 14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. • Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper. • According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector. 15. Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. • Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper. • We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution. • For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review. 16. Declaration of LLM usage Question: Does the paper describe the usage of LLMs if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the core methods in this research? Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required. Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve the development of any LLMs, nor their use beyond minor editing. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components. • Please refer to our LLM policy in the NeurIPS handbook for what should or should not be described.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.18598v1 [cs.CV] 13 Oct 2026 Rethinking Projector Training in Multimodal LLMs Fabian Gröger † † thanks: Joint first authorship Affiliation: EPFL Affiliation: University of Basel Affiliation: HSLU Naël Ouerghemi 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: EPFL Shuo Wen 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: EPFL Maria Brbić Affiliation: EPFL Abstract Multimodal LLMs are typically trained by first aligning a vision encoder with a language model via projector training on large image-caption datasets, followed by joint training of the full multimodal model. Despite its widespread use, the role of the projector training stage remains poorly understood. We find that (i) using only 10 10 to 20 % 20\% of the data for training the projector already recovers most downstream performance gains, and (ii) projectors trained on different datasets can be linearly interpolated while largely preserving performance. These results suggest that projector training mainly performs a coarse alignment, which many different projectors achieve equally well. Motivated by these findings, we propose PORTAL , a training-free projector initialization that requires neither paired image-caption data nor gradient-based optimization , but only per-modality summary statistics. PORTAL computes an optimal-transport-based map between Gaussian approximations of the vision and language feature distributions on a shared principal subspace, so that the projector training stage can be skipped entirely. Without any paired data, PORTAL matches the standard pipeline trained on 558k image-caption pairs across six LLM backbones, two vision encoders, and 16 benchmarks. It outperforms that pipeline in 3 3 of 7 7 (vision encoder, LLM) settings and reaches an average 98 % 98\% of its score across the other four. 1 Introduction Modern multimodal LLMs commonly align a vision encoder with a language model by first training a projector on a large amount of image-caption paired samples, followed by joint training of the full multimodal model. This pipeline has become standard, from LLaVA [ 1 , 2 ] , Molmo [ 3 ] , and InternVL [ 4 ] to the QwenVL series [ 5 ] . While the first stage of projector alignment has been motivated by the goal of producing a visual tokenizer compatible with the frozen LLM [ 1 ] , what this stage actually does remains poorly understood. Prior works offer conflicting evidence: Prismatic [ 6 ] reports that skipping projector alignment can improve performance, whereas Cambrian-1 [ 7 ] shows that scaling the training data of projector alignment to 2.5M image-caption pairs helps. MM1 [ 8 ] suggests that factors like resolution and data mixing matter more than the projector design. These findings are difficult to reconcile without a deeper understanding of what projector alignment actually does. In this work, we show that projector alignment primarily performs coarse alignment , mapping visual features into a language-model-compatible input space which admits a large set of possible solutions. Two empirical observations support this view: (i) using only 10 10 to 20 % 20\% of the standard 558 558 k-sample alignment corpus achieves similar performance to training on the full dataset, and (ii) projectors trained on entirely different datasets can be linearly interpolated without losing performance. If the projector alignment learned a precise and semantically unique mapping, neither reducing the training data nor linear interpolation between independently trained projectors would preserve performance. Figure 1 : Projector alignment as a coarse alignment with a broad solution space. ( Left ) Standard pipeline: during projector alignment, the vision encoder and language model are frozen, and only the projector is trained to map visual tokens into a representation space compatible with the LLM using image-caption pairs. ( Middle ) We show that projectors trained on different image-caption datasets can be linearly interpolated while largely preserving downstream performance, indicating that there is a large solution space for the weights of the projector. ( Right ) This observation motivates a closed-form solution of projector alignment. We propose a training-free projector PORTAL constructed by optimal transport between the two modalities’ marginal statistics. Motivated by these observations, we propose PORTAL ( P rojector via O ptimal-transpo RT AL ignment), a training-free approach that constructs the projector from the marginal statistics of the two modalities. PORTAL is the Bures-Wasserstein optimal transport map between Gaussian approximations of the vision feature distribution and the language-model input distribution, computed in a shared top- k k principal subspace. It does not require any paired captions or gradient-based optimization , relying only on the per-modality means, principal directions, and the spread along each direction. PORTAL removes the projector alignment training stage entirely. Across seven (vision encoder, LLM) pairs spanning four LLM families (Vicuna, LLaMA, Qwen, OLMo) from 0.5B to 8B parameters, and two vision encoders (CLIP, SigLIP), PORTAL matches the standard pipeline trained on 558 558 k image-caption pairs and exceeds it in three out of seven settings, peaking at 106 % 106\% of the trained baseline. When PORTAL is used to initialize rather than replace projector alignment, the performance of the baseline is reached with 135 × 135\times fewer alignment FLOPs. Performance gaps are concentrated on OCR-heavy benchmarks, where marginal statistics appear insufficient to capture fine-grained character-level spatial structure that paired supervision provides. 2 Related Work Projector alignment in multimodal LLMs. Two-stage multimodal LLM training, where a vision encoder is first aligned to a frozen language model via training a projector, followed by visual instruction tuning, has become a standard pipeline for training multimodal LLMs. This pipeline was popularized by LLaVA [ 1 , 2 ] and replicated in InstructBLIP [ 9 ] , BLIP-2 [ 10 ] , Flamingo [ 11 ] , Molmo [ 3 ] , InternVL [ 4 ] , and the Qwen-VL series [ 5 ] . Despite its success, the role of Stage-I projector alignment has been poorly understood and prior studies offer conflicting views. Prismatic finds it can be skipped without a loss [ 6 ] . Cambrian-1 reports that scaling Stage-I data to 2.5M pairs helps [ 7 ] . MM1 emphasizes resolution and data mixing over the projector itself [ 8 ] . We resolve this disagreement by identifying what projector alignment actually does: Stage-I acts as geometric conditioning of visual features into the LLM input distribution , not as fine-grained semantic learning. This explains the three findings above as a single phenomenon: skipping Stage-I works when the projector already lands in a compatible region (Prismatic [ 6 ] ), more data helps only until that region is reached (Cambrian-1 [ 7 ] ), and the resolution and data mixing dominate because they affect the conditioning more than the projector capacity does (MM1 [ 8 ] ). These findings lead us to propose a closed-form projector that requires neither paired data nor gradient updates. Connector designs and projector geometry. Beyond the MLP used in LLaVA [ 1 ] , connector architectures span the Q-Former [ 10 ] , Perceiver Resampler [ 11 ] , locality-enhanced abstractors [ 12 ] , ALIGN [ 13 ] , vision-expert mixtures [ 14 ] , prefix-attention adapters [ 15 ] , and pixel-shuffle or patch-merging schemes for token reduction [ 16 , 5 ] . A complementary line of work analyzes what these connectors actually do. Verma et al. [17] track how visual information degrades through LLM layers, Li et al. [18] probe information loss through learned projectors, Li and others [19] report systematic norm discrepancies between visual and text tokens, and Shukor and Cord [20] show that cross-modal alignment emerges primarily after self-attention layers. We use the 2-layer MLP projector of LLaVA by default, and also test PORTAL with a linear projector and with the C-Abstractor [ 12 ] , which has 19 × 19\times more parameters (Section 5.3 ). Optimal transport for feature alignment. The Bures-Wasserstein optimal transport map between two Gaussians has a closed form on positive-definite covariances [ 21 , 22 ] , which the construction of the projector in our work exploits. Courty et al. [23] introduced OT for domain adaptation, and Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola [24] used Gromov-Wasserstein to align word-embedding spaces with no paired anchors. Closest to PORTAL is CORAL [ 25 , 26 ] , which aligns second-order statistics with a single linear map for domain adaptation. PORTAL extends this idea to the multimodal-alignment setting and ties it explicitly to the Bures-Wasserstein optimum on a shared top- k k principal subspace, which we then use as a closed-form projector rather than a regularizer. Training-free and efficient connector construction. Several recent works try to eliminate or reduce connector training. VPGTrans [ 27 ] transfers a learned visual prompt generator across LLMs at reduced cost. LangBridge [ 28 ] interprets visual tokens as combinations of language embeddings, enabling cross-LLM transfer at the price of bottlenecking visual information through a vocabulary subspace. SEMI [ 29 ] meta-learns a hypernetwork connector that adapts to new modalities from a few samples. In the related CLIP-classification setting, training-free or lightweight adapters such as Tip-Adapter [ 30 ] and TaskRes [ 31 ] cache or residualize over a frozen backbone. PORTAL differs from all of the above by requiring neither paired data, gradient steps, learned caches, nor a vocabulary bottleneck: it is a closed-form construction from per-modality summary statistics alone. Gupta et al. [32] also learn without paired multimodal data, but to improve a unimodal representation by sharing parameters across unpaired modalities, whereas we ask whether the projector between a frozen vision encoder and a frozen LLM needs paired training at all. 3 What Does the Projector Alignment Actually Do? 3.1 Projector Alignment Saturates with a Small Number of Samples To investigate the role of projector alignment, we first examine how downstream performance scales with the amount of Stage-I training data. If strong performance requires large-scale data, it would suggest the projector is learning fine-grained visual-language correspondences. Conversely, if a small fraction of the data is sufficient, this would indicate that the projector primarily learns a coarse-grained correspondence, placing visual features into a broadly compatible input space for the language model. We conduct this analysis on the LLaVA 1.5 setup (CLIP ViT-L/14-336, Vicuna 1.5 7B, 2-layer MLP projector), with LCS-558k for Stage-I and LLaVA-665k for Stage-II. For the data-fraction experiment we replace Vicuna with MobileLLaMA 1.4B, which keeps 11 data fractions on two corpora tractable. We evaluate on 16 benchmarks grouped into four categories adapted from the Cambrian-1 [ 7 ] taxonomy: Knowledge (Know.), General (Gen.), OCR, and Vision-Centric (Vis.). Appendix C lists the benchmarks in each. Full experimental details are in Appendix C.1 . (a) LCS-558k (b) ShareGPT-1.2M Figure 2 : Stage-I gain saturates early. Relative gain in downstream performance over the no-pretraining baseline by Cambrian-1 category, as a function of Stage-I data fraction on LCS-558k (left) and ShareGPT-1.2M (right). OCR and Chart benefit the most, while Knowledge and Vision-Centric scores saturate early. We observe that only 10 10 to 20 % 20\% of the LCS-558k image-caption pairs already capture most of the downstream benefit, and all categories plateau by 30 30 to 40 % 40\% (Figure 2 ). The marginal downstream benefit of the remaining pairs is small under this protocol. ShareGPT-1.2M, more than twice as large, does not do better: its average peaks at 38.1 38.1 with 40 % 40\% of its data (Appendix D ). These results suggest that projector alignment is not primarily learning fine-grained visual-language correspondences. Rather, it appears to perform a coarse-grained alignment step, mapping visual features into a region of the LLM input space from which subsequent joint training can effectively adapt the full multimodal model. 3.2 Projector Alignment Admits a Broad Solution Space We have shown that projector alignment can be achieved with only a small fraction of the standard pretraining data.
